title: RZD • Sanatorium Booking System
subtitle: Turning a complex internal process into a predictable booking flow
coverAlt: RZD sanatorium and resort booking service cover

facts.label: scope
value: UI system for a reusable internal service

facts.label: audience
value: RZD employees and their families across eligibility tiers

facts.label: focus
value: Predictability, trust, and repeat usage under operational constraints

value.text: The sanatorium & resort booking service is a benefits platform inside the RZD employee ecosystem — covering 500+ resorts nationwide, available to employees and their families across different eligibility tiers. On paper, the service was functional. In practice, it was consistently underutilized in a way internal metrics didn't fully capture.

The risk wasn't user drop-off during booking. It was behavioral: a service that costs real organizational capital to build and maintain, but fails to become a habit, is a structural problem — not a UI problem. That reframing shaped everything that followed.

The service wasn't broken in terms of functionality. It was broken in terms of predictability — which is a harder problem because it doesn't surface as a clear error state. Users entered with genuine intent and left without confidence. Not because booking was impossible, but because the system provided no framework for decision-making: which resorts applied to their eligibility tier, what would happen after submission, whether the approval process had defined timelines.

Each unknown added a small tax on trust. Collectively, those taxes meant the service felt risky rather than reliable. The real diagnostic signal was this: even users who successfully completed a booking didn't return. Conversion wasn't the problem. Retention was.

Redesigning within an enterprise internal system means accepting constraints that would be unacceptable in a greenfield product. The business rules — subsidies, quota allocation, tiered eligibility, approval chains — were fixed. Multiple backend systems couldn't be consolidated. No control over core logic. Manual approval processes remained manual.

The tradeoff I had to accept upfront: I couldn't simplify the underlying complexity. The risk was that trying to hide it would create a different failure mode — users encountering the complexity later in the flow with no framework to interpret it. The mitigation was to make the system legible instead of pretending it was simple.

The mental model shift that unlocked the design direction: this is not a booking flow, it's a trust-building system. The target isn't conversion at the end of a single session — it's repeat usage over multiple years. That reframe changed what "good" looked like. A booking flow optimizes for completion. A trust system optimizes for predictability at every step, including the steps after submission and the steps where the answer is "pending approval" or "not available this season."

I mapped the service as overlapping journeys rather than a single linear flow. Price-sensitive users, location-first users, eligibility-constrained users, returning users — they share a system but diverge at critical decision points. Those divergence points were exactly where the existing design failed. They became the design targets.

value.alt: Information architecture and audience-specific journeys for the sanatorium booking service
value.caption: Before designing screens, I mapped the service as a decision system: information architecture, user types, and expectation failures were laid out explicitly so the interface could respond to real behavioral divergence instead of hiding it under one generic flow.

value.alt: Wireframe set for search, filtered results, card, and booking form
value.caption: These wireframes were not visual drafts. They were a way to test whether the service stages remained legible as one coherent logic: entry, comparison, selection, eligibility, and booking had to connect without forcing users to reinterpret the system at each step.

value.alt: Readable service flow with loops and decision points
value.caption: I treated the service as a set of overlapping journeys with shared rules and different failure points. That made it possible to design for real loops, branch conditions, and recovery paths instead of pretending the booking process was linear.

value.text: Moving eligibility validation earlier was the highest-leverage change. In the original flow, users discovered their eligibility constraints late — sometimes after selecting a resort and filling a form. The failure mode was clear: wasted effort, eroded trust. The risk in moving it earlier was top-of-funnel friction. The mitigation was framing it as orientation rather than restriction — the system telling you what's available to you, not what you can't have.

value.caption: The comparison layer was designed to reduce interpretation work. Instead of making users open multiple pages and reconstruct differences manually, the system externalized the decision criteria and turned comparison into a supported action.

value.text: Making comparison a first-class action addressed a subtler problem. Users were mentally comparing resorts across multiple sessions, tabs, and phone calls with colleagues — because the system didn't support that process. The tradeoff was scope: a proper comparison layer adds complexity to both the interface and the backend. The decision was to invest here because decision confidence is directly linked to trust in the outcome. If you feel uncertain when you choose, you're more likely to abandon the service before committing.

value.alt: Booking flow with explicit steps and expectations
value.caption: The booking form was used to expose system logic early: constraints, eligibility, required inputs, and next steps became part of the interface. This reduced the feeling of a black box and made submission feel like a predictable step rather than a risky guess.

value.text: System transparency throughout the booking and approval process was the least glamorous but most structurally important change. Status visibility, explicit next steps, expected timelines — these things are invisible when they work. But they're the mechanism through which a single successful booking becomes a reason to return. Without them, every interaction resets the trust counter to zero.

value.alt: Main page of the sanatorium booking service with structured entry points and curated selections
value.caption: The main page was redesigned as a structured entry point, not a decorative homepage. Its job was to orient users, shorten the path to relevant options, and reduce the cognitive cost of entering a complex service for the first time.

value.text: To hold the interaction model together visually, I built a minimal design system — typography, spacing, and core interface elements structured around repeated states and content patterns. That wasn't a visual polish decision. It was an operational one: a service with this many branches and states only stays learnable if it behaves consistently across all of them.

value.alt: Design system foundations and component structure for the sanatorium booking service
value.caption: I built the UI on top of a minimal but explicit system of typography, spacing, and reusable interface elements. That was important not for visual polish, but for operational consistency: repeated states, steps, and content patterns had to behave as one learnable product.

value.text: The service became a structured system that explains itself. Users can compare resorts on defined criteria, understand their eligibility before investing effort, follow a booking process with explicit stages and expected outcomes, and track status after submission without ambiguity. The underlying complexity didn't disappear — the quotas, approvals, and eligibility tiers still exist. What changed is that the system now has a consistent framework for communicating all of that, so the complexity becomes learnable rather than unpredictable.

value.alt: Status tracking interface for booking progress
value.caption: Trust does not end at submission. This status layer was designed to keep the system legible after the user acts, so waiting, approval, and document handling remain understandable instead of becoming a silent operational gap.

value.alt: Detailed booking status and outcome tracking
value.caption: Outcome visibility was treated as part of the service itself. By making progress, decisions, and next actions explicit, the system could close the loop properly and give users a reason to rely on it again in the future.

value.text: The primary behavioral shift: from one-time risky interaction to repeatable system usage. Users who previously treated the service as something to avoid began treating it as something to plan around. The design work that's hardest to measure — status transparency, recovery flows, early eligibility framing — is also the work most responsible for that shift. Trust is built in the moments where the system could have failed silently but didn't.

The instinct in enterprise service design is to simplify relentlessly: reduce options, flatten flows, minimize decisions. For complex benefit systems with real eligibility rules and operational dependencies, that instinct is often wrong. Users don't want a simpler system. They want a system they can predict.

The distinction matters because it changes what you optimize for. Simplification removes information. Legibility structures it. One makes the system easier to complete once. The other makes it possible to rely on.
